opus-5.5.text:
So the thing we really wanted to get at with FrontierMath is the kind of reasoning that you can't shortcut by pattern-matching against things you've seen before. A lot of existing math benchmarks, things like GSM8K or even MATH, were largely saturated, and part of the concern was that the problems look a lot like problems that exist somewhere on the internet, so a model can do quite well by recognizing a familiar template and running through a known procedure.

What we wanted instead were problems where you have to actually combine ideas in a novel way. A typical problem might require you to understand some fairly deep concept from, say, algebraic geometry or number theory, recognize that it connects to some other area, and then carry out a long chain of nontrivial steps to get to a concrete answer. The kind of thing where a professional mathematician working in that specialty might need hours, sometimes days, to solve it, and where someone outside the specialty might not even know where to start.

We also designed them so the answers are hard to guess. They're typically big, specific numbers or objects that you can verify automatically, so you can't just get lucky or reason your way to a plausible-looking answer. You actually have to do the work. And we made sure the problems were new and unpublished, so there's no contamination from training data.

So the creative reasoning we're after is really something like: can you find the right approach when there's no obvious template, can you bring together tools from different areas, and can you sustain that over a long, careful derivation without making errors. That's much closer to what doing actual mathematical research looks like, and I think it's a much more informative signal about whether these systems are developing genuinely deep reasoning capabilities, rather than just getting better at reproducing things they've already seen.

r001.rationale: The response says the benchmark should test combining ideas in novel ways, including connecting concepts across mathematical areas and bringing together tools from different areas.

r002.rationale: The response describes the capability being tested but does not state that AI has so far made limited progress at creatively combining ideas.

fable-5.1.text:
So the thing we were worried about with existing math benchmarks is that they'd basically saturated. GSM8K, the MATH dataset, even a lot of the competition-style problems — frontier models were getting into the 90s, and at that point you're not learning much from the benchmark anymore. And a lot of what's left is either contamination or just noise in the grading.

So with FrontierMath, the idea was to go to the other end of the distribution. We worked with something like sixty mathematicians — people who are actually research mathematicians, in some cases Fields Medalists helped us look at the problems — and we asked them to write problems that are genuinely hard. Not hard in the sense of "this requires a clever trick a well-prepared olympiad student would know," but hard in the sense that a professional in that subfield might take hours or days to work through it.

And the kind of reasoning we're trying to get at — I'd say it's a few things. One is the ability to bring together ideas from different areas. A lot of the problems aren't solvable by just knowing one technique really well. You have to notice that, say, something from number theory connects to something in algebraic geometry, or that a combinatorial object has a structure you can exploit analytically. That's the sort of thing mathematicians would describe as creative — the recognition of a non-obvious connection.

The second is sustained multi-step reasoning where you have to hold a lot of structure in your head and not drop the ball. Some of these problems have a large number of steps, and an error anywhere along the way means you get the wrong answer. And the answers are designed to be automatically verifiable — they're specific numbers or objects — so you can't guess your way there, and you can't get partial credit for something that sounds plausible.

And then the third thing, which I think is maybe underrated, is just the ability to work on something you haven't seen before. We were very careful about contamination — the problems are new, they're not on the internet, and we keep them private. So if a model does well, it's not because it memorized a solution. It's because it actually did the mathematics.

I'd be honest that we don't fully know what "creativity" means in this context — it's partly an empirical question we're hoping the benchmark helps answer. When we released it, the best models were solving around two percent. And the interesting thing is watching which problems fall first, and whether that tracks the kind of reasoning mathematicians think is hard, or whether it tracks something else entirely.

r001.rationale: The response says some problems require connecting ideas across mathematical areas and calls recognizing a non-obvious connection a form of creativity.

r002.rationale: The response reports that the best models solved around two percent of the benchmark overall, but does not say AI has made limited progress specifically in creatively combining ideas.

astra-6.text:
We want to test whether a model can come up with the key idea that makes a difficult problem tractable. That might mean finding a useful representation, introducing an auxiliary construction, or noticing a connection to another area of mathematics. Once you have that insight, the remaining steps might be fairly routine—but finding it is the hard part.

So we’d like problems where you can’t simply recognize a familiar template and apply a standard procedure. You have to explore different approaches, understand why some of them fail, and find a way forward. That gets closer to the kind of creative reasoning involved in doing mathematics, rather than just executing a calculation.

r001.rationale: The response mentions noticing a connection to another area of mathematics, but does not say the benchmark should test creatively combining disparate ideas from the mathematical literature.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that AI has shown limited progress in creatively combining ideas.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d like it to test the ability to come up with a useful idea when it isn’t obvious which approach to take. In a difficult mathematics problem, you might need to find a clever construction, introduce an auxiliary object, or notice a connection to a different area of mathematics. Once you have that insight, carrying out the proof might be relatively straightforward. But finding the insight is the hard part.

So we want problems where you can’t just recognize a familiar template and execute a standard procedure. You have to explore possible approaches, recognize when one isn’t working, and find a different way of looking at the problem.

r001.rationale: The response says solvers may notice a connection to another area of mathematics, but it does not identify connecting disparate ideas from the mathematical literature as the ability to test.

r002.rationale: The response makes no claim about AI’s progress or its ability to combine ideas creatively.
